Lewis Hall is England's best left-back - because the Newcastle player started out as a midfielder in Chelsea's youth teams
Lewis Hall excelled for England in their win over Spain in Madrid and is belatedly establishing himself as first-choice left-back. With insight from the man who played him as a midfielder during his youth career at Chelsea, Adam Bate picks out a key reason for the player's rise...
Wednesday 18 November 2026 11:17, UK
The most spectacular moment came in the 18th minute. It took a fifth Spain player to stop him dancing through the defence. But it was the turn away from Fabian Ruiz and Mikel Merino on the seven-minute mark that showed Lewis Hall at his most impudent.
The situation seemed dangerous for England but Hall looked so comfortable in a central role. His performance in the 3-2 win in Madrid highlighted his quality with and without the football. In the first half, he completed five dribbles. Five more than Lamine Yamal.
He deserved to be at the World Cup in the summer. Most would have picked the Newcastle player but, unfortunately for Hall, the England head coach Thomas Tuchel was not among that number. They went into the tournament with arguably only one specialist left-back.

Ironically, however, those who know Hall best might not put him in that category either. In fact, that little pirouette that so befuddled Spain's World Cup winners had been a feature of his game when he was a youngster at Chelsea. He was no left-back as a kid.
"A lot of the time I was playing a 3-4-2-1 formation with 10s," Ed Brand tells Sky Sports. "I would put him as a 10 quite a bit because he had always been a central midfield player. If I played a 4-2-3-1 formation then I would play him as one of the 6s or the 8s instead."
Brand worked with Hall as head coach of Chelsea's Under-18 side when the player was among the youngest in the side at just 16. "What a good kid he is." So impressed was Brand that shifting him out to the left flank was merely a way of keeping him in the side.
"There were players who were older than him. Good players," he explains. "In certain games, where I wanted to keep him in the team, he might have to play at left wing-back even though I knew at that point it was not his favourite position. He was a midfielder."
He recalls one particular game away to Tottenham when he played him as an out-and-out full-back. "I was going to him, 'Look, this is how I will fit you in.' I just wanted 11 footballers in every position because we wanted to make sure we got on the ball." The rest is history.
"He started to play there a little bit more, a little bit more, and it just went from there. Now he is seen in most football fans' eyes as a left back. Whereas I know that growing up, he has always been an attacking player with the ability to get goals and run beyond."
Brand points to the key role of Andy Myers in developing Hall as a left-back at under-21 level. His game evolved. "He was excellent when he was a 10. But people adapt and see your football differently." And Hall's schooling in midfield still helps him.
"He is so comfortable at left-back because of where he is used to playing. When you are a player with his ability, used to playing in the centre of the pitch, seeing the game 360, you get moved to full-back, you look at it and think it is easy. He can see everything."
Brand talks of a player "showing all his attributes" and as seen against Spain he is hardly restricted to the touchline. "Full-backs in the modern game are so important with how they invert inside, they do a lot of stuff infield anyway. With his talent, he excels there."
Of course, the test against Lamine Yamal is off the ball as well as on it. Hall had mixed experiences against Barcelona's boy wonder earlier this year. Excellent in the home leg of Newcastle's Champions League tie, he was part of the side that conceded seven away.
At 22 years old, Hall is still learning himself. But he showed in Madrid that he is more than capable of doing the other side of the game. His attacking assets elevate him above most players in his position but he is certainly not a weak link defensively either.
"What is so impressive about Lew is how much he has improved upon his defensive side," agrees Brand. "You cannot play in the Premier League and not be able to defend to a certain level, He will continue to get better the more exposure he gets to that."
There will be more exposure, of that there is no doubt. His omission in the summer is ever more startling but the caps will keep coming now and an exciting club career is ahead of Hall too. A big test awaits in the Premier League against champions Arsenal on Saturday.
For Brand, there is pride at his development already and enthusiasm about his potential to improve even more. The former Chelsea midfielder has turned himself into England's outstanding left-back. "He has done brilliantly," concludes his former youth coach.
"In time, he will be one of those England internationals whose name will be one of the first on the sheet. I am biased but I already think there is a big enough case for it." After this latest showing in an England shirt, everyone, even Tuchel, is starting to agree.
